Carbon Monoxide
Carbon monoxide is a very localized air quality problem caused almost exclusively by motor vehicle exhausts. CO is emitted from vehicular sources resulting in a complex latticed pattern corresponding closely to highway networks. These tail-pipe level emissions are also particularly sensitive to low-level radiation inversions, resulting in very strong daily and seasonal cyclic variations.
Despite the large tonnage of CO emissions, the Federal and State one-hour CO standards in the Bay Area have not been exceeded in the current decade. However, the Federal 8-hour average standard of 9 ppm has been frequently exceeded in some areas. The major excess area is the Santa Clara Valley, centered on San Jose and extending to Sunnyvale. There is a small secondary maximum over Vallejo, and isolated urban-center cases at San Francisco, Oakland, and San Rafael. These National Standards are not to be exceeded more than once a year. Since this standard is exceeded, the Bay Area has been designated a non-attainment area by EPA.
To explain the above pattern, one must examine the seasonal and daily cycles in the data. In the past 6 years, there has been no CO excess from March through August. Over 80% occur in November, December, and January. On a daily basis over 90% of these 8-hour excesses occur between 4 p.m. and 2 a.m. There is an intense but short maximum from 7 to 9 a.m., followed by low levels from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Then, since the winterseason formation of surface-based radiation inversions corresponds to the evening traffic maximum, the sustained build-up of high CO levels occurs. There is also a day-of-week factor, with greatest frequency of excesses on Friday, the maximum vehicle use day. Typically, the District's highest CO values are recorded near 11 p.m. on Friday nights in downtown San Jose. Hopefully, this targeting of the excesses in time and space may suggest the most precise and cost-effective control strategies.
The Santa Clara Valley shows a strong "drainage pool" effect. That is, the light surface winds under the radiation inversion drain downslope (as water would) and collect pools of contaminants.
Since emissions are projected to increase significantly from 1975-2000, it would appear that carbon monoxide will continue to be a problem unless additional regional controls are adopted.
